questions.q: What specific prophecy do the astrologers make about the ten-day-old prince Jung Jung Bahadur, and how does the infant respond?
questions.a: The astrologers predict the prince will die because he was born in the hour of the Bull, and the Bull and Tiger are enemies — so death will come from a tiger. The infant responds by speaking clearly: "All those who are born will one day have to die... There would be some sense in it if you could tell us the manner of that death," and then growls, "Let tigers beware!" A wrong answer (e.g., "the infant cried" or "the astrologers predicted death by lion") reveals the student has not read the opening scene closely and misses the establishment of the Maharaja's defining traits: intellectual arrogance and defiant aggression from birth.

questions.q: Why does the Maharaja ban tiger hunting by everyone except himself, and what does this reveal about his understanding of "self-defence"?
questions.a: He bans others to monopolize tiger kills for his tally of 100. He twists the saying "You may kill even a cow in self-defence" to justify killing tigers as "self-defence" against the prophecy. A wrong answer (e.g., "to protect tigers" or "because he loved hunting") shows the student confuses the Maharaja's stated pretext with his actual motive — exposing a failure to distinguish between a character's rhetoric and their true psychological drive.

questions.q: Apply the "STEAL" characterization method (Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks) to the Maharaja's interaction with the British officer's secretary. What does this episode reveal about his political pragmatism versus his obsession?
questions.a: Steps: (1) Speech: He refuses the officer's request firmly ("tiger hunt! That's impossible!"). (2) Thoughts (inferred): He fears other officers will demand the same. (3) Effect: The officer's wife accepts 50 diamond rings; the Maharaja pays 3 lakh rupees. (4) Actions: He bribes to keep his throne AND his tiger quota. (5) Looks: Not described, but his "loud crack of laughter" later shows performative confidence. This reveals he sacrifices state wealth (pragmatism) to protect his personal obsession — a wrong answer focusing only on "he was brave" misses the transactional, fearful calculus underneath.

questions.q: Analyze the contrast between the Maharaja's public titles (e.g., "His Highness Jamedar-General, Khiledar-Major, Sata Vyaghra Samhari...") and his private death caused by a two-anna wooden toy. What satirical point does Kalki make through this disparity?
questions.a: The titles project invincibility, divine authority, and martial glory ("Tiger King", "Visva Bhuvana Samrat"). The death — from a sliver on a cheap, poorly carved wooden tiger — reduces him to absurd vulnerability. Kalki satirizes how power constructs grandiose self-images that crumble before trivial, uncontrollable reality. A wrong answer listing titles without linking to the wooden tiger's irony shows the student sees details but not the structural contrast that drives the satire.

questions.q: Evaluate: Is the Maharaja a tragic hero whose flaw (hubris) leads to his downfall, or a purely satirical figure constructed to mock authoritarianism? Defend your judgment with three textual arguments.
questions.a: He is a satirical figure, not a tragic hero. Arguments: (1) No catharsis — his death is grotesque and darkly comic (surgeons announce success, then "The Maharaja is dead"), not dignified. (2) No self-awareness — he never questions the prophecy's logic or his morality; he only calculates. (3) The world doesn't mourn — the dewan hides a tiger, hunters cover up his miss, the shopkeeper overcharges; the system survives him. A wrong answer calling him "tragic" because "he tried hard" ignores the text's consistent mocking tone and the absence of noble stature.

questions.q: Create a diary entry dated the night before the Maharaja's 100th tiger hunt, written in his voice. It must reflect his internal conflict: the astrologer's warning about the 100th tiger, his exhaustion, and his refusal to show fear.
questions.a: A strong entry will: (1) Use first-person, imperious yet anxious tone ("I, the Tiger King..."). (2) Reference the astrologer's exact warning ("beware the hundredth"). (3) Show physical weariness ("ten years, seventy tigers, now this last beast eludes me"). (4) End with performative resolve ("Tomorrow I finish what destiny began"). A poor entry will sound like a modern student ("I'm stressed about my project") or ignore the prophecy's psychological weight, revealing the student cannot inhabit the character's historical and psychological context.
